# Results — Study 600 (Asset Location)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **"put the
bonds in the tax-deferred account and the stocks in taxable; it adds real after-tax return for
free"** (the textbook asset-location rule, Dammon-Spatt-Zhang 2004) — tested on a 60/40
household with a 50/50 taxable/traditional-IRA split, simulated one calendar year at a time over
every overlapping 30-year cohort of the Shiller long tape, plus one modern SPY/IEF low-rate
cohort. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number. As-of **2026-07-03**; only **complete calendar years** enter (the long tape's last
populated year is 2022; the modern tape's is 2025 — no partial years, ever). Fingerprints:
long tape `254d1e72f9f7`, modern tape `97c3a1b86d4f`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Long tape | Shiller monthly S&P 500 price / dividend / GS10 (datasets/s-and-p-500 mirror of Shiller's `ie_data`), 1,830 months 1871-01 → 2023-06 (rows with populated dividend + yield) → **151 complete calendar years 1872–2022** of annual components |
| Modern tape | yfinance SPY (stock sleeve) + IEF (7-10y Treasury fund, bond sleeve): **unadjusted** closes + cash distributions → **23 complete years 2003–2025**, income and price legs split exactly as a brokerage statement splits them |
| Household | 60/40 stock/bond, 50/50 taxable/traditional-IRA, 30-year horizon; baseline rates **24% ordinary / 15% LTCG+QDI**; equity fund turnover **10%/yr** (realised at LTCG, average-cost basis, loss carryforward); bond-fund price gains realised annually; IRA taxed once at withdrawal at the ordinary rate; taxable settles LTCG on terminal unrealised gains |
| Policies | `bonds_ira` (the rule), `stocks_ira` (the anti-rule), `pro_rata` (every account holds 60/40) — same pre-tax 60/40, same funds, annual rebalance (free inside the IRA) |
| Execution lag | **one, documented**: the bond coupon for year *t* is the **prior-December** 10y yield — the yield the household could actually see when it allocated |
| Inference | overlapping annual-start 30-year cohorts are massively serially dependent → **Newey-West (HAC) *t* with lag = 29** on the mean cohort delta and on the delta-on-yield regression |

## The signal — bonds-in-IRA vs stocks-in-IRA, 122 overlapping 30-year cohorts (1872–1993 starts)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| after-tax annualised, bonds-in-IRA | **6.84%/yr** (mean across cohorts) |
| after-tax annualised, stocks-in-IRA | 6.66%/yr |
| after-tax annualised, pro-rata | 6.76%/yr |
| **delta: bonds-in-IRA − stocks-in-IRA** | **+17.78 bps/yr** · HAC *t* (lag 29) = **+3.55** · win rate **86.9%** |
| **delta: bonds-in-IRA − pro-rata** | **+8.55 bps/yr** · HAC *t* (lag 29) = **+3.11** · win rate **82.8%** |
| cohort delta range | −14.46 to +59.14 bps/yr |
| mean terminal after-tax wealth gap | **+5.19%** more wealth after 30 years, same funds, same risk |

The rule is **real on the tape**: putting the bonds in the IRA beats putting the stocks there by
**+17.8 bps/yr of after-tax return** on average — **HAC *t* = 3.55**, clearing the desk's
*t* ≥ 2 bar — and beats the no-thought pro-rata default by +8.6 bps/yr (*t* = 3.11). Over a
30-year horizon that compounds to **~5.2% more terminal wealth** while holding the identical
pre-tax 60/40 in the identical funds. The tape is index-level (Shiller composite + constant-
maturity 10y Treasury): no survivor panel is involved.

## Costs — the location choice itself is free

All three policies hold the same two funds and rebalance once a year; only the *placement*
differs. Average taxable trade volume: bonds-in-IRA **2.67 %NAV/yr**, stocks-in-IRA
**2.41 %NAV/yr**, pro-rata **3.34 %NAV/yr**. Charging **5 bps one-way × NAV** on the
*differential* volume moves the headline delta by **+0.013 bps/yr** — three orders of magnitude
below the +17.8 bps/yr signal. Capacity is unbounded and the vehicle (an IRA plus a taxable
brokerage account) is the default retail setup.

## The benefit scales with the yield level

| cohort-average locked coupon | mean delta (bps/yr) | n |
|---|--:|--:|
| Q1 (lowest yields, 3.06% avg) | +12.38 | 31 |
| Q2 (3.70%) | +12.53 | 30 |
| Q3 (4.42%) | +11.55 | 30 |
| Q4 (highest, 7.44% avg) | **+34.30** | 31 |

Regression of the cohort delta on the cohort's mean coupon: **+5.57 bps/yr per 1pp of yield**
(HAC *t* = +67.8 — near-mechanical, as the arithmetic predicts: the whole benefit is annually-
taxed coupon income sheltered by the IRA). Low-yield decades shrink the prize toward ~12 bps/yr;
they do **not** flip it at baseline settings.

## Tax-rate grid — mean delta (bonds-in-IRA − stocks-in-IRA), bps/yr

| ordinary \ LTCG | 15% | 20% |
|---|--:|--:|
| 22% | +10.77 (*t* = +2.26, win 77.0%) | −9.95 (*t* = −1.84, win 31.1%) |
| 24% | **+17.78 (*t* = +3.55, win 86.9%)** | −3.16 (*t* = −0.57, win 46.7%) |
| 32% | +47.43 (*t* = +7.68, win 100%) | +25.54 (*t* = +4.09, win 91.0%) |
| 37% | +67.47 (*t* = +9.62, win 100%) | +44.96 (*t* = +6.56, win 100%) |

Every **realistic 2026 US bracket pair sits on the positive diagonal** — 22/15, 24/15, 32/15,
37/20 — because the 20% LTCG rate only begins inside the top ordinary brackets. The negative
cells (22/20, 24/20) are instructive but not real US household configurations: they show the
rule's engine is the **wedge** between the ordinary rate and the LTCG rate, and a narrow wedge
kills it. The benefit is strongly increasing in the bracket: a 37/20 household pockets
**+45 bps/yr**, a 22/15 household **+11 bps/yr**.

## Third axis — when does the rule flip? (equity-turnover sweep, long tape)

| equity turnover | mean delta (bps/yr) | HAC *t* | win % | lowest-yield-quartile delta |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0% (buy-and-hold stock) | +26.27 | +4.15 | 98.4% | +17.89 |
| **10% (headline, index fund)** | **+17.78** | **+3.55** | **86.9%** | **+12.38** |
| 25% | +11.32 | +2.58 | 77.9% | +7.31 |
| 50% | +5.72 | +1.40 | 68.9% | +2.36 |
| 100% (active fund) | **−0.29** | −0.07 | 53.3% | **−3.69** |

**It flips — exactly where the arithmetic says it must.** The rule assumes equities are the
tax-*efficient* asset; crank their turnover to 100% (an active fund distributing its gains every
year) and the equity deferral advantage vanishes: the mean delta crosses **zero** (−0.3 bps/yr,
*t* = −0.07) and goes outright negative (−3.7 bps/yr) in low-yield cohorts. At ≥50% turnover the
benefit is already statistically indistinguishable from zero (*t* = 1.40). The rule is
**conditional**: bonds-in-IRA is free money *for index-fund equity holders*, and quietly wrong
for high-turnover active holders in low-rate decades.

## Modern low-rate cohort — SPY + IEF, 2003–2025 (23 complete years)

Mean bond income yield **2.90%** — the low-rate regime the "it no longer matters" objection
points at. After-tax annualised: bonds-in-IRA **7.51%**, stocks-in-IRA **7.09%**, pro-rata
**7.31%** → delta **+41.68 bps/yr** vs stocks-in-IRA, **+19.49 bps/yr** vs pro-rata (single
cohort — no *t*; the long tape carries the inference). Turnover sweep on this cohort: +53.67
(0%) → +41.68 (10%) → +33.54 (25%) → +27.81 (50%) → +23.12 bps/yr (100%) — positive throughout,
because this window's equity capital gains were huge and its bond price leg was small.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful

Deterministic seeded worlds, **averaged over 20 seeds** (no single-seed baseline):

| world | mean delta (bps/yr) | sd | n seeds |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **null: zero tax rates** | **+0.000** | 0.000 | 20 |
| planted coupon 2% | +15.105 | 5.366 | 20 |
| planted coupon 4% | +21.000 | 6.097 | 20 |
| planted coupon 6% | +29.585 | 7.079 | 20 |

With zero tax rates the account boundary is meaningless and the simulator returns a delta of
**exactly 0.000** across all 20 seeds — it cannot manufacture a location benefit out of nothing.
The planted bond-coupon knob scales the measured delta monotonically (15 → 21 → 30 bps/yr).
*(Machinery proof only — never cited in support of the Signal stamp.)*

## Roth reversal — the untested corner that flips the sign (skeptic check, 2026-07-04)

The whole simulator models a **traditional** IRA: the tax-advantaged account is taxed once at the
ordinary rate on withdrawal (`(ira_s + ira_b) * (1 - ordinary)` at terminal settlement). That is
the Dammon-Spatt-Zhang setup. A **Roth** IRA is withdrawn tax-free — change only that one terminal
line to `* 1.0` and re-run the identical 122 cohorts (the traditional baseline reproduces
`+17.78 bps/yr`, `t = +3.55` in the same script, so the reimplementation is faithful):

| account type (baseline 24/15, turnover 10%) | bonds-in-IRA − stocks-in-IRA | HAC *t* | win % |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Traditional** (the study) | **+17.78 bps/yr** | +3.55 | 86.9% |
| **Roth** | **−28.57 bps/yr** | **−3.15** | **10.7%** |

The rule **inverts** for a Roth: bonds-in-Roth *loses* to stocks-in-Roth by −28.6 bps/yr, and the
reversal is statistically strong (*t* = −3.15, cohort range −95.8 to +21.6, win only 10.7%). The
mechanism is standard (Reichenstein; Kitces): a tax-*free* wrapper should shelter the asset with
the largest sheltered dollar-gains — the 30-year compounded equity leg — not the bond coupon. In a
*traditional* account the terminal ordinary tax claws back a share of that equity growth (the
government owns ~24% of the IRA), which neutralises the "shelter the big grower" advantage and lets
the annual-coupon-drag argument win — hence bonds-in-traditional. The Roth reversal deepens with
turnover (−21.3 at 0% → −43.9 bps/yr at 100%) and holds across brackets (−30.8 at 22/15, −33.3 at
37/20). "Put bonds in the IRA" is therefore only correct advice once you specify *which* IRA — and
Roth IRAs are a mainstream retail vehicle the study never tested.

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL (traditional IRA).** Bonds-in-IRA beats stocks-in-IRA by **+17.78 bps/yr** of
  after-tax return across 122 overlapping 30-year cohorts, **HAC *t* (lag 29) = +3.55**, win rate
  86.9%; vs the pro-rata default **+8.55 bps/yr** (*t* = +3.11). Compounds to **+5.2% terminal
  wealth** at identical pre-tax risk. Positive at every realistic 2026 US bracket pair (+11 to +67
  bps/yr). Index-level tape — no survivorship. The signal is genuine and reproduces exactly; it is
  honestly scoped to the **traditional / tax-deferred** IRA that Dammon-Spatt-Zhang model.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE (downgraded from Investable, skeptic pass 2026-07-04).** The location
  choice does cost **nothing** (differential rebalancing +0.013 bps/yr, unbounded capacity) — but
  the "free lunch for a plain retail household on the default retail setup" claim is **conditional
  on the account being a traditional IRA**. Point the identical rule at a **Roth** IRA and it
  reverses to a **−28.6 bps/yr penalty** (*t* = −3.15, win 10.7%), worse at higher turnover. The
  earlier stamp read the sign as universal; it is not. A retail household that holds a Roth and
  follows "bonds in the IRA" *loses* tens of bps a year. Real and free for the traditional-IRA
  household modelled here; a trap if mis-applied — hence Fragile, not Investable.
- **"When does it flip?" — CONFIRMED (it flips on two axes, and we found both lines).** (1) At
  **100% equity turnover** the long-tape delta crosses zero (−0.29 bps/yr, *t* = −0.07; −3.69
  bps/yr in lowest-yield cohorts) and at ≥50% turnover it is statistically zero (*t* = 1.40) —
  the rule is conditional on holding **tax-efficient equity**. (2) At **Roth vs traditional** the
  rule inverts outright (−28.6 bps/yr, *t* = −3.15) — the larger and more common flip. Low yields
  only shrink the prize (Q1 +12.4 vs Q4 +34.3 bps/yr); they do not flip it alone.
